name: Shila Devi Temple
deity: Durga in her form as Shila Devi
significance: A Shakti shrine inside Amer Fort near Jaipur, established in 1604 by Raja Man Singh I, with carved pillars and an image cut from a black stone slab. It is a major centre of worship during Navratri and part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.
story: Man Singh I is said to have been divinely instructed to retrieve the goddess from the sea at Jessore, and the image was carved from the stone slab, or shila, that he recovered.

name: Jeen Mata Temple
deity: Jeen Mata (Jayanti Mata), a form of Shakti
significance: A hilltop Shakti shrine in the Shekhawati region of Sikar district, built of marble and limestone, which Wikipedia dates by tradition to around the 8th century. An eternal flame is said to have been kept burning at the shrine for centuries.
story: When soldiers of Aurangzeb's time approached the hill a swarm of bees is said to have driven them off, after which the goddess became known as Bhanwaron ki Devi, the goddess of the bees.

name: Rani Sati Temple
deity: Rani Sati, also called Narayani Devi
style: White marble with murals and glass mosaics
significance: The largest temple in India dedicated to Rani Sati, a Rajasthani woman said to have lived between the 13th and 17th centuries. It is built of white marble and decorated with wall paintings, murals and glass mosaic work.
story: Tradition holds that Rani Sati was a rebirth of Narayani Devi, who avenged her husband Tandhan's killing by a king before immolating herself on his pyre.

name: Sachiya Mata Temple
deity: Sachiya Mata, also called Shri Osiya Mataji
significance: A goddess temple at Osian in Jodhpur district, as old and as important as the neighbouring Mahavira Jain temple and carrying decorative features of Jain workmanship. She is honoured as the protective deity of the Oswal community.
story: Jain tradition says the teacher Ratnaprabhasuri turned the fierce goddess Chamunda into the vegetarian deity Sachiya Mata, who then became guardian of the Oswals.

name: Mahavira Jain Temple, Osian
deity: Mahavira, the twenty-fourth Tirthankara
significance: Built in 783 CE under the Gurjara-Pratihara king Vatsaraja, this is described as the oldest surviving Jain temple in western India and an important tirtha, especially for the Oswal and Maheshwari communities.
story: Jain tradition holds that miracles worked by Acharya Ratnaprabhasuri converted the villagers of Osian, after which the goddess Chamunda became the temple's guardian deity.

name: Kaila Devi Temple
deity: Kaila Devi, worshipped as Mahalakshmi and Mahayogini
significance: A marble Shakti temple in the hills of Karauli district, founded by Maharaja Gopal Singh of the Jadaun house and completed in 1730. It draws large crowds to its annual Kaila Devi fair.
story: A yogi's bullock cart carrying the goddess's image is said to have halted in the forested hills, and by divine ordinance the image was installed at that very spot.

name: Sanwaliyaji Temple
deity: Krishna, worshipped as Sanwaliya Seth
significance: A Krishna temple at Mandphiya in Chittorgarh district, regarded as second only to Shrinathji at Nathdwara among Vaishnava pilgrimage sites in the region and drawing devotees from Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat.
story: In 1840 a cowherd named Bholaram is said to have dreamt of three divine images buried at Bagund village; the three that were unearthed were enshrined at three nearby sites, of which Mandphiya became the principal shrine.

name: Charbhuja Temple, Garhbor
deity: Krishna, worshipped as Charbhuja Nath
style: Shikhara temple with a tall spire over the sanctum
significance: A Krishna temple at Garhbor in the Kumbhalgarh tehsil of Rajsamand district, about 32 km from Kumbhalgarh, whose 85 cm four-armed image holds conch, discus, mace and lotus. Its main observances are Fagotsav, Janmashtami and Annakut.

name: Sahasra Bahu Temples (Sas-Bahu), Nagda
deity: Vishnu (Sahasra Bahu, 'one with a thousand arms')
significance: A pair of ruined stone temples at Nagda, an early capital of Mewar near Udaipur, lavishly carved inside and now protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. Their local name Sas-Bahu is a corruption of Sahasra Bahu.

name: Harshat Mata Temple
deity: Harshat Mata, worshipped as Lakshmi
significance: A ruined early-medieval temple beside the Chand Baori stepwell at Abhaneri, laid out in panchayatana plan with a main shrine and four subsidiary shrines. Art historians debate whether it was originally a Vaishnava or a Durga shrine before becoming the shrine of Harshat Mata.

name: Neelkanth Temple, Alwar
deity: Shiva, worshipped here as Neelkanth
significance: A hill temple in an isolated valley beside Sariska National Park in Alwar district, built by the local Pratihara feudatory Parmeshwara Mathanadeva. Its sculpture, including erotic panels, is compared to the work at Khajuraho.

name: Tanot Mata Temple
deity: Tanot Mata (Aavad Mata), regarded as a form of Hinglaj Mata
significance: A desert shrine in Jaisalmer district close to the Pakistan border, founded in 828 CE by the Bhati Rajput king Tanu Rao and now also serving as a war memorial cared for by border troops.
story: During the 1965 war some three thousand shells are said to have fallen on the temple without exploding, and the 1971 victory at nearby Longewala is locally credited to the goddess's protection.

name: Kapil Muni Temple, Kolayat
deity: Kapila, the Vedic sage
significance: A pilgrimage town in Bikaner district built around a desert lake ringed by 52 bathing ghats, marble temples and sandstone pavilions, centred on the sage Kapila. Its Kartik fair draws thousands of pilgrims and doubles as a camel market.
story: Kapila is believed to have shed his body here beneath a peepal tree, and bathers hold that the lake washes away sin.

name: Bhandasar Jain Temple
deity: Sumatinatha, the fifth Tirthankara
style: Red sandstone, five-ratha sanctum with shikhara
significance: A three-storey Svetambara Jain temple in Bikaner built in red sandstone with yellow-stone carving, famous for its frescoes, leaf paintings and mirror work depicting the lives of the twenty-four Tirthankaras. It is a protected monument of the Archaeological Survey of India.
story: Local tradition claims that forty thousand kilograms of ghee were used instead of water in mixing the mortar for the temple.

name: Kiradu Temples
deity: Shiva (the best-preserved Someshvara temple); a Vishnu temple also stands at the site
significance: A group of five ruined Hindu temples in the Thar Desert near Barmer, built by vassals of the Chalukya monarchs and richly carved with animal and human figures. An inscription of 1178 CE records repairs to a temple damaged during Ghurid raids.

name: Chandrabadani Devi Temple
deity: Sati, worshipped through a Shri Yantra carved on stone
significance: A Siddhpeeth on a Garhwal Himalayan ridge at about 2,277 m in Tehri district, where the goddess is worshipped not as an image but as a Shri Yantra carved into a flat stone. An annual fair is held in April.
story: The site is held to be where the torso of Sati fell as Shiva carried her body, her weapons scattering across the hill, which iron tridents at the shrine are said to recall.

name: Purnagiri Temple
deity: Maa Purnagiri, a form of Sati
significance: A Shakti Peeth on a hill near Tanakpur in Champawat district, at about 910 m, drawing thousands of pilgrims each year, above all during Chaitra Navratri in March and April.
story: The shrine is held to mark the spot where the navel of Sati fell as Shiva carried her body across the world.

name: Baleshwar Temple
deity: Shiva, known here as Baleshwar
significance: A stone temple complex at Champawat, an early capital of the Chand dynasty, renowned for its carving and accompanied by shrines to Ratneshwar and Champawati Durga. A copperplate inscription records the reconstruction being completed by Hari Chand in 1423.

name: Kasar Devi Temple
deity: Kasar Devi, a form of Durga
builtDisplay: rebuilt 1948; shrine traced to 2nd c. CE
significance: A ridge-top shrine near Almora set among huge rock formations, with a cave-like sanctum, an eternal flame and a continuously burning dhuni. The present structure was built in 1948, and the site drew Swami Vivekananda in the 1890s and later became a landmark of the Hippie trail.

name: Mukteshwar Dham Temple
deity: Shiva
significance: A Shiva temple on the highest point of Mukteshwar in Nainital district, from which the hill town takes its name. The cliffs beside it, known locally as Chauli-ki-Jali, are a well-known viewpoint.

name: Gurdwara Paonta Sahib
deity: Dedicated to Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru
significance: A gurdwara on the bank of the Yamuna founded by Guru Gobind Singh in 1685, where he stayed some four and a half years, longer than anywhere else, and composed a large body of writing. It is also the birthplace of his eldest son, Sahibzada Ajit Singh.
story: The name comes from paon, foot, and tika, became stable, recalling that the Guru's horse halted at this spot.

name: Gurudwara Manikaran Sahib
deity: Associated with Guru Nanak, the first Sikh Guru
significance: A gurdwara in the Parvati valley of Kullu district, standing beside hot springs that Sikh tradition connects with Guru Nanak's visit during his third udasi. The spring water is used to cook langar and the site is revered by Sikhs and Hindus alike.
story: Sikh tradition holds that Guru Nanak caused the hot springs to appear so that food could be cooked for the community kitchen.

name: Ranchhodrai Temple, Dakor
deity: Ranchhodrai, the Trivikrama form of Vishnu, identified with Krishna
significance: A major Krishna pilgrimage temple in Kheda district, built between 1769 and 1772 by the Pune Brahmin Gopal Tambvekar, with four gold-capped shikharas and seven domes inside fort-like walls beside the Gomti lake. It is a leading centre of Pushtimarg Vaishnava worship in Gujarat.
story: Devotees hold that the image was miraculously carried from Dwarka to Dakor by the devotee Bodana in 1151.

name: Shamlaji Temple
deity: Shamlaji, Vishnu in his Trivikrama form, also called Gadadhara Vishnu
significance: A major Vaishnava pilgrimage centre on the Meshwo river in Aravalli district. The site was already an important religious centre in the sixth century and probably housed a sculpture workshop whose work travelled far across western India; the present temple dates from the 15th-16th centuries.

name: Bahucharaji Temple
deity: Bahuchara Mata
significance: A major Shakti pilgrimage centre in Mehsana district that gives the town of Becharaji its name, now managed by the state government and equipped with guesthouses and dharamshalas for pilgrims. Its great fair falls on the full moon of Chaitra.

name: Chamunda Mata Temple, Chotila
deity: Chamunda Devi
significance: A hilltop shrine to Chamunda on Chotila hill in Surendranagar district, reached by a climb of some 920 steps and one of the busiest Shakti shrines in Saurashtra.

name: Jalaram Temple, Virpur
deity: The saint Jalaram Bapa, together with the images of Rama, Sita, Lakshman and Hanuman he worshipped
builtDisplay: shrine at the saint's house, 19th c.
significance: A shrine in the house complex at Virpur where the saint Jalaram Bapa (1799-1881) lived, preserving his belongings and the images he worshipped. It is unusual among Indian temples in having refused all offerings since 9 February 2000, and draws crowds at Jalaram Jayanti.
story: The temple displays the jholi and danda that Jalaram is said to have received from God himself.

name: Akshardham, Gandhinagar
deity: Swaminarayan
style: Traditional Hindu temple architecture in pink Rajasthan sandstone, designed by Chandrakant Sompura
significance: A 23-acre BAPS Swaminarayan complex in Gandhinagar built without steel or iron, from 6,000 tonnes of pink sandstone, with 97 carved pillars, 17 domes and 264 sculpted figures around a gold-leafed image of Swaminarayan. It also houses exhibition halls, gardens and a water show.

name: Nishkalank Mahadev Temple
deity: Shiva, present as five Shivalingas
significance: A Shiva shrine standing out in the Arabian Sea off Koliyak in Bhavnagar district, reachable on foot only at low tide and submerged when the tide returns. Maha Shivratri and Navaratri draw large numbers of pilgrims.
story: The Pandavas are said to have installed five Shivalingas here on Krishna's instruction to expiate the sins of the Mahabharata war.

name: Koteshwar Temple
deity: Shiva, as a four-foot self-manifested lingam; also called Kotilingeshwar
style: Stone temple with three domes in the porch and a black marble shrine
significance: An ancient Shiva site near the mouth of Kori Creek at the western edge of Kutch, some 178 km from Bhuj and 4 km from Narayan Sarovar. The present structure dates from 1820, and the site was noted by the seventh-century Chinese traveller Xuanzang.
story: Ravana is said to have been given the lingam by Shiva and to have dropped it here, whereupon it multiplied so that the original could not be told apart, giving the place its name of ten million gods.

name: Narayan Sarovar
deity: Trikamray (Vishnu), with shrines to Lakshminarayan, Adinarayan, Govardhannath, Dwarkanath, Lakshmiji and Kalyanray
style: Domed temples in the manner of the Dwarka shrines
significance: One of the five sacred lakes of Hinduism, the Panch-Sarovar, in Lakhpat taluka of Kutch. Its main temples were built in 1734 by Vagheli Mahakunvar, wife of Rao Deshalji I, with the Kalyanray temple added in 1828.
story: The Saraswati river is said to have reached the sea near this spot, which is what made the lake holy.

name: Mata no Madh (Ashapura Mata Temple)
deity: Ashapura Mata, patron goddess of Kutch
significance: The shrine of Ashapura Mata, household deity of the Jadeja rulers and patron goddess of Kutch, first built in the 14th century by the ministers Ajo and Anagor and rebuilt in 1823 after the 1819 earthquake. Thousands come during Navaratri.
story: Soldiers of Mian Ghulam Shah Kalhoro are said to have been struck blind when they attacked the temple in 1762, and their ruler donated a great bell when their sight returned.

name: Rukmini Devi Temple
deity: Rukmini, chief queen of Krishna and an incarnation of Lakshmi
style: Richly carved, with narathara and gajathara panels at the base of the tower
significance: A carved temple about 2 km outside Dwarka housing a marble image of Rukmini holding conch, discus, mace and lotus. Local custom holds that a pilgrimage to Dwarka is complete only after worshipping here.
story: The Skanda Purana explains the temple's distance from Krishna's own shrine by the curse of the sage Durvasa, who condemned the couple to live apart for twelve years after Rukmini offered water to Krishna before him.

name: Hutheesing Jain Temple
deity: Dharmanatha, the fifteenth Tirthankara
significance: A white marble Jain temple in Ahmedabad built in 1848, begun by Hutheesing Kesarisinh and completed under his widow Harkunwar, with 52 subsidiary shrines around the main temple and a 78-foot Manastambha added for Mahavira's 2500th birth anniversary. It was raised during a severe famine and employed hundreds of artisans for two years.

name: Taranga Jain Temple
deity: Ajitnatha, the second Tirthankara
style: Maru-Gurjara, with bhumija and sekhari elements in the shikhara
significance: A hill tirtha in Mehsana district whose main temple, built in 1161 by the Solanki king Kumarapala under the guidance of Acharya Hemachandra, holds a 2.75 m white marble image of Ajitnatha. The site has separate Svetambara and Digambara compounds with nineteen temples between them.
story: The name is locally traced to a shrine of the goddess Tara said to have been built by an ancient Buddhist king.

name: Girnar Jain Temples
deity: Neminath (Arishtanemi), the twenty-second Tirthankara
builtDisplay: main temple rebuilt 1129 (Sajjana, under Jayasimha Siddharaja)
significance: A cluster of Jain temples on Mount Girnar in Junagadh district, built in grey granite with marble carving. The Neminath temple was rebuilt in 1129 by Sajjana, governor under Jayasimha Siddharaja, the Ambika temple predates 784 CE, and further shrines were added by merchant patrons in the 15th century. The site is one of the Svetambara Pancha Tirth.
story: Neminath is said to have renounced the world after seeing animals penned for slaughter at his own wedding feast, and to have attained omniscience and moksha from Girnar's highest peak.

name: Kayavarohan Temple (Lakulish)
deity: Shiva in the form of Lakulisha, as a black stone lingam
dynasty: Modern restoration on an ancient site
significance: A Shaiva centre at Karvan in Vadodara district, regarded as the birthplace of Lakulisha, the second-century revivalist of the Pashupata school, and counted among the sixty-eight Shiva pilgrimage sites. Its lingam bears the image of a meditating yogi holding parchments and a citron, and the temples were restored in the late twentieth century by Kripalvanand.
story: The name is read as kaya, body, plus avarohan, descent: the place where the Lord's body descended.

name: Gop Temple
deity: Surya, the sun god, with Vaishnava, Skanda and Shaiva imagery also present
style: Unusual variant of the Nagara style, with a square plan, pyramidal shikhara and corbelled construction
significance: Standing on the Vartu river in Jamnagar district, this is one of the earliest surviving stone temples in Gujarat and the earliest in Saurashtra, radiocarbon-dated to about 550 CE. It is a Monument of National Importance.

name: Shankheshwar Parshwanath Jain Temple
deity: Parshwanatha, the twenty-third Tirthankara
significance: A leading Jain pilgrimage centre in Patan district. The present Parshwanath temple was built in 1811, but Jain temples are recorded at Shankheshwar from at least 1155 CE, and ruins of an older temple dated 1596 stand nearby.

name: Aundha Nagnath Temple
deity: Shiva, as the Nagnath Jyotirlinga
significance: A Shiva temple at Aundha in Hingoli district, Marathwada, counted as the eighth of the twelve Jyotirlingas.
